answer: A spinlock makes a waiting thread busy-wait: it keeps looping, checking whether the lock is free, instead of going to sleep. That burns CPU cycles doing nothing useful, and on a single CPU it can even stop the lock holder from running and releasing the lock. In a real-time system this is bad because the time a task can spend spinning is hard to bound, so it hurts predictability and can delay higher-priority work. Spinlocks are only reasonable when locks are held for a very short time on multiprocessors, where spinning is cheaper than a context switch.

answer: Under this prevention scheme, if a process holding some resources requests another one that can't be granted immediately, it's preempted: all the resources it currently holds are released. Those preempted resources are added to the list of resources the process is waiting for, and it's restarted only when it can get back its old resources along with the new one. This breaks the no-preemption condition, one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock, because resources can now be taken away from a waiting process. It works well for resources whose state is easy to save and restore, like CPU registers or memory, but not for things like printers.

answer: External fragmentation is when there's enough free memory in total for a request, but it's split into small scattered holes, so no single hole is big enough, say three free 100 KB holes when a process needs 250 KB. Compaction fixes this by moving the allocated blocks together so all the free memory forms one big contiguous block. But it only works if relocation is dynamic, done at execution time, because the processes' addresses change when they move. It's also expensive, and there's an I/O problem: a job doing I/O into its buffer can't be moved, so it has to be latched in memory, or the I/O has to go through OS buffers.

answer: In a multilevel feedback queue there are several ready queues with different priorities, and the scheduler always serves the highest-priority non-empty queue, so a lower queue only runs when all the higher queues are empty. What makes it 'feedback' is that processes move between queues based on their behaviour: a process that uses its whole time slice is moved down, so CPU-bound jobs sink while I/O-bound and interactive jobs stay high, and a process that waits too long can be moved up to prevent starvation.

answer: FIFO keeps the pages in memory in a queue in the order they were loaded. When a page fault happens and all frames are full, it evicts the page at the head of the queue, the one that has been in memory the longest, loads the new page and puts it at the tail.
